headline: Weather Balloon Company Lands Big Air Force Deal

levels.label: Grade 3-4
levels.summary: A company called WindBorne makes special balloons that fly high in the sky without any pilot or engine. These balloons collect information about the weather, like temperature and wind. WindBorne has about 700 of these balloons flying all over the world right now. The United States Air Force decided to buy weather information from these balloons. This deal could be worth almost $50 million, which is a huge amount of money. The Air Force will only pay for the information it actually needs, a little bit at a time. WindBorne also uses a smart computer program, kind of like artificial intelligence, to study all the balloon data and guess what the weather will do next. This can help people get ready for storms. Recently, WindBorne even flew a balloon into the middle of a typhoon, which is a giant, dangerous storm, to gather information that could help keep people safe. This deal shows that even small companies can do big, important work for the government by using new ideas and technology.

levels.label: Grade 5-6
levels.summary: WindBorne Systems, a startup based in California, builds autonomous weather balloons, meaning they fly and steer themselves without a pilot. The company currently has about 700 of these balloons floating around the planet, gathering details about the atmosphere like temperature, humidity, and wind. Now the U.S. Air Force has agreed to buy this weather data in a contract that could be worth up to $49 million. The Air Force won't pay everything right away; instead, it will order data whenever it needs information about a specific place or time. So far, it has spent $1.7 million, but more orders are expected. This money will help WindBorne grow its fleet of balloons and improve how they work. The data doesn't just go to the government, though. WindBorne also feeds it into its own computer program that uses artificial intelligence, or AI, to predict the weather. This is a newer way of forecasting compared to older methods that used supercomputers to calculate physics equations. Interestingly, the contract was given to WindBorne without other companies competing for it, because officials decided WindBorne was the only company able to do this specific job well enough. The company recently made history by flying a balloon with no engine straight into the eye of a typhoon, a powerful storm, to collect rare data. This shows how new technology, like AI and smart balloons, is changing the way we predict dangerous weather and keep people safe.

levels.label: Grade 7-8
levels.summary: WindBorne Systems, a startup headquartered in Redwood City, California, has signed a major agreement with the U.S. Air Force that could bring in nearly $50 million. The company operates roughly 700 autonomous weather balloons, devices that fly on their own and collect real-time data about the atmosphere, such as temperature, pressure, and wind patterns. Instead of paying the full amount upfront, the Air Force will purchase data as needed, ordering readings from specific regions and time periods. So far, it has spent $1.7 million, with more purchases expected as the partnership continues. Notably, this contract was awarded without competitive bidding, meaning no other companies got to compete for it. Officials decided WindBorne was uniquely capable of providing this kind of global atmospheric data in the way the military required. The funding will help WindBorne expand its balloon fleet and improve its hardware, while also supporting the company's artificial intelligence-based weather forecasting system. WindBorne recently released an updated version of this AI model, which the company claims is now more accurate than the long-standing forecasting system used by the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts. That traditional method relies on supercomputers solving complex physics equations, while WindBorne's approach uses machine learning, feeding years of historical weather data into a computer program that learns patterns and makes faster predictions. This shift toward AI-driven forecasting has become increasingly common across the industry, including at major tech companies like Google DeepMind, whose models are now helping guide U.S. hurricane response. One standout achievement for WindBorne came in August, when it became the first organization to send an engineless balloon into the eye of a typhoon, a feat that required both an accurate weather model and enough balloons in position to make the risky maneuver possible. Rather than using motors, these balloons steer by changing altitude, releasing air, or dropping sand used as ballast weight, allowing them to catch winds that carry them toward their destination. This contract highlights how private companies and the military are increasingly relying on cutting-edge technology to understand and predict weather, which matters for everything from military operations to disaster preparedness and public safety.

levels.label: Grade 9-10
levels.summary: WindBorne Systems, a weather technology startup based in Redwood City, California, has secured a contract with the U.S. Air Force that could be worth up to $49 million, marking the largest deal in the company's history. Founded in 2015, WindBorne operates a fleet of roughly 700 autonomous weather balloons that continuously collect atmospheric data from around the globe, including measurements of temperature, humidity, wind speed, and pressure. Rather than paying the full sum immediately, the Air Force will purchase data incrementally, placing orders for specific regions and timeframes as operational needs arise. So far, only $1.7 million has been spent, but company executives anticipate steady growth in orders moving forward. Notably, the contract was awarded without competitive bidding, a decision that reflects the government's conclusion that WindBorne was the only company capable of delivering this type of global data collection to meet the Air Force's particular specifications. According to WindBorne's co-founder and chief technology officer, Andrey Sushko, the funding will primarily support expanding the balloon fleet and advancing research into improving the hardware's performance. The money comes shortly after WindBorne raised $37 million in a separate funding round over the summer, signaling strong investor confidence in its growth trajectory. Beyond government contracts, WindBorne uses its collected data to power its own artificial intelligence weather forecasting model, called WeatherMesh 6. The company claims this latest version outperforms the long-established forecasting system used by the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts, which relies on supercomputers to simulate atmospheric physics through complex equations. By contrast, WindBorne's AI model is trained on decades of historical weather data, allowing it to identify patterns and generate forecasts more quickly than traditional physics-based simulations. This approach reflects a broader shift happening across the meteorology field, as machine learning models developed by major research labs and government agencies increasingly rival or exceed the accuracy of conventional forecasting tools. Google DeepMind, for example, has developed cyclone-tracking AI tools that are becoming central to how U.S. officials prepare for and respond to hurricane season. One of WindBorne's most notable recent achievements came in August, when it became the first organization to fly an engineless aircraft directly into the eye of a typhoon to gather atmospheric readings. Since the balloons lack engines, they navigate by adjusting altitude, releasing air, or dropping ballast made of sand, allowing wind currents to carry them toward specific destinations. According to Sushko, this maneuver required both a sophisticated predictive model and a large enough constellation of balloons positioned strategically around the storm, representing one of the first instances where an AI model directly informed a real-world operational decision in weather tracking.

levels.label: Grade 11+
levels.summary: WindBorne Systems, a California-based startup founded in 2015, has secured a contract with the U.S. Air Force worth up to $49 million, the largest in the company's history, to supply atmospheric data collected by its fleet of autonomous weather balloons. The company currently operates approximately 700 of these unpowered, self-navigating balloons worldwide, gathering empirical sensor readings on temperature, humidity, pressure, and wind that feed both into commercial sales and WindBorne's proprietary artificial intelligence forecasting model. Structured as a pay-as-needed arrangement, the contract allows the Air Force to order region- and time-specific data rather than committing to a lump sum; thus far only $1.7 million in orders have been placed, though executives anticipate continued growth. Significantly, the contract was awarded without competitive bidding, reflecting a government determination that WindBorne was the sole entity capable of delivering this particular global data-collection capability under the military's operational requirements. Co-founder and CTO Andrey Sushko indicated that the funds will primarily support expansion of the balloon constellation alongside continued research and development to refine hardware performance. This federal windfall follows closely on the heels of a $37 million Series B funding round WindBorne raised over the summer, underscoring sustained investor confidence as the company scales its operations. Central to WindBorne's value proposition is its AI-driven forecasting system, WeatherMesh 6, released earlier this year, which the company asserts now surpasses the accuracy of the long-dominant model maintained by the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF). That traditional approach relies on supercomputers executing physics-based simulations of atmospheric behavior, an intensive and expensive computational process. WindBorne's deep-learning alternative instead trains on decades of accumulated weather data, enabling end-to-end pattern recognition that can generate forecasts with greater speed, though not without tradeoffs. Industry observers note that the emergence of transformer-based architectures, combined with ECMWF's release of extensive historical datasets several years ago, has catalyzed a broader transformation in meteorology, with AI models developed by frontier technology labs and government agencies increasingly rivaling or surpassing conventional forecasting methods. Even so, the field remains a mixed landscape, as both approaches currently retain distinct strengths, necessitating their combined use for comprehensive weather analysis. Google DeepMind's recent cyclone forecasting advancements, for instance, are becoming increasingly integral to how U.S. agencies coordinate hurricane season responses. Perhaps WindBorne's most striking technical milestone came in August, when it became the first organization to direct an engineless flight vehicle into the eye of a typhoon to collect in-situ data. Lacking any propulsion system, these balloons navigate purely through altitude adjustments, controlled air release, or the jettisoning of sand ballast, techniques that allow operators to exploit prevailing wind patterns to steer toward desired locations. Sushko characterized this achievement as dependent on two converging factors: sufficiently sophisticated predictive wind models capable of informing navigation decisions, and a constellation large enough to ensure balloons were strategically positioned when the opportunity arose. He further noted that this represented one of the first instances in which a deep-learning model directly informed a live operational decision in atmospheric science, a development with implications extending well beyond this single contract toward the future architecture of global weather intelligence.

questions: How might better and faster weather forecasts change the way your family or community prepares for storms, hurricanes, or extreme weather?
Do you think it's fair for the government to give a big contract to one company without letting other companies compete for it? Why or why not?
As artificial intelligence gets better at tasks like predicting the weather, what other important jobs do you think AI could take on in the future, and how might that affect people's careers?
